claims.text: Ethanol-oxidation pathway selectivity in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs is governed by atomic-scale elemental disorder.
Atomic-scale disorder modulates the d-band centers of the constituent metals.
A more random elemental distribution corresponds to higher configurational entropy.
Higher configurational entropy weakens the binding of poisoning intermediates such as CO*.
Weaker CO* binding favors a complete, non-CO ethanol-oxidation pathway over partial oxidation.
Rapid quenching of nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs produces a highly disordered solid solution.
Thermal annealing promotes elemental ordering and reduces configurational entropy in PtPdRhRuIrOs.
The proposed annealing treatment can increase ordering while preserving the nanoscale structure.
The local atomic environment determines the distribution of d-band centers at active sites.
Annealing-induced ordering narrows the distribution of d-band centers.
A broader distribution of d-band energies in the disordered catalyst provides sites with lower CO* binding strength.
Lower CO* binding reduces active-site poisoning.
Annealing-induced atomic order shifts d-band centers toward values that strengthen intermediate adsorption.
Stronger intermediate adsorption in the ordered catalyst promotes incomplete ethanol oxidation.
The rapidly quenched catalyst will exhibit lower operando CO* adsorption signals than the annealed catalyst.
The rapidly quenched catalyst will produce more CO2 than the annealed catalyst.
The rapidly quenched catalyst will have greater selectivity for complete ethanol oxidation than the annealed catalyst.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate-temperature fuel-cell ethanol-oxidation conditions if nanoscale structure is preserved.
Other Pt-based high-entropy alloys provide prior evidence that electronic-structure modification can reduce CO* binding and improve non-CO pathway selectivity.
Direct evidence linking disorder-driven d-band modulation to ethanol-oxidation selectivity in PtPdRhRuIrOs has not been established.
